summary:
AER is a Marswalk planner for the first astronauts on Mars, with a survival game inside it. It layers real NASA data over Jezero Crater, where Perseverance landed: HiRISE images and elevation, THEMIS thermal inertia, MEDA weather and Mastcam-Z dust measurements. An astronaut can plan a walk there and see what it will cost in oxygen, CO₂ scrubber capacity, cooling water and battery, and the latest moment they can turn back and still reach shelter.

The game shows why each layer matters. A meteor strike forces a lone astronaut to crash-land in Jezero with a dead radio. They scavenge supplies and scrap, repair their lander into a base, then reach Perseverance to call Earth for help, before their own exhaled CO₂, the cold or a dust storm stops them. Every number in the suit comes from NASA physiology and spacesuit data. The challenge asks for a hyperlocal map that keeps an explorer safe while they do science; AER turns that map into decisions the player can feel.
details:
Live app: https://aer-black.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/ZektoxFx/aer

WHAT IT DOES

AER helps a Mars astronaut answer one question before every surface walk: can I get there and back alive, and what will it cost?

- A hyperlocal layered map of a 6.4 × 4 km area of Jezero Crater, from the Octavia E. Butler landing site to the western delta front: a HiRISE photo mosaic, shaded relief and slope from the HiRISE elevation model, a THEMIS thermal-inertia layer that flags likely soft sand, and real Perseverance hardware, sample sites and the rover's traverse.

- Route costing: click waypoints and the route finds a walkable path around steep ground, with distance, time and the cost in oxygen, scrubber, water and battery. Past its point of no return the route turns red and the map says TURN BACK BY that time. A green line shows how far you can go and still get home.

- A 3D view built from the real HiRISE elevation (hills drawn 1.6× taller, labelled on screen). The astronaut walks it in first or third person, and every step feeds the same suit simulation.

- Survival scenarios that teach real hazards: scrubber saturation (on Mars the danger is your own breath), a dust storm with a five-minute countdown and a choice of shelter, and "work hot, rest cold" (walking spends cooling water even at −55 °C; resting through a −75 °C night brings on hypothermia within about three hours).

- The story: a meteor strike, a crash-landing, scavenging and repairs (including salvaging real Mars 2020 hardware), then reaching Perseverance to call Earth through a real orbiter relay pass from NASA's Mars Relay Network Handbook.

HOW IT WORKS

- Suit simulation in TypeScript, checked by automated tests. Oxygen, CO₂ and scrubber use come from one metabolic rate set by speed, slope and load, following NASA's ISS-era averages (0.84 kg O₂ and 1.0 kg CO₂ per person per day). A 300 W walk matches the Apollo moonwalk average. Starting supplies match Apollo and ISS spacesuit figures.

- Point of no return: the planner simulates the walk out minute by minute, and at each minute simulates the walk back with uphill and downhill swapped. On a long flat walk it is about 3½ hours with a fresh suit, and about 1¼ hours with the partly used scrubber the crash leaves behind.

- Weather and light: temperature, pressure and wind from Perseverance MEDA for the chosen sol; the sun follows Jezero's latitude and season; sunlight under dust from NASA's Mars solar radiation model (TM-103623) with the albedo Perseverance measured at Jezero (0.12).

- Dust storms drive solar power and panel dust (capped at the 2% per sol highest ever observed). The game's storm is deliberately stronger than Jezero's real January 2022 storm (τ 1.38); its peak is based on the 2018 global storm that ended Opportunity.

- Data pipeline: Python scripts read only the needed parts of multi-gigabyte USGS HiRISE files and bake everything into static files, so the app runs anywhere with no live service.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Mission planning: NASA's Mars maps are regional or global. AER works at the scale of a single walk and turns the data into the numbers a crew needs: cost, margin and when to turn back.

- Learning: the scenarios make invisible risks concrete, such as why breathing harder doesn't help when the scrubber fails, and why a dust storm is dangerous for darkness and lost power, not wind.

- Honest about its limits: every chart names its mission, instrument and sol; game fiction and design values are labelled.

- Goal: a tool that could grow into a crew planning aid, where any Mars site with NASA data becomes a walkable, costed map.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite and three.js for the app; Vitest for tests; Python (NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, tifffile) for the data pipeline; ffmpeg; GitHub; Vercel.

CREATIVITY AND WHAT WE CONSIDERED

We made the map something you can feel: every metre walked, every kilogram carried and every storm costs oxygen in a simulation built on NASA numbers. We checked every value against its source, labelled fiction as fiction, and kept the real data archived and credited (never "live").
